big_idea: FREQUENCY TABLES list categories with their COUNTS. Qualitative = words. Quantitative = numbers.
learning_intention: We are learning to build a frequency table.
student_learning_goal: I can build a frequency table with qualitative or quantitative data.
success_criteria: I can ask a survey question.
I can build a FREQUENCY TABLE.
I can distinguish QUALITATIVE and QUANTITATIVE data.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Detective Dot and Tally — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Tally: Favourite drink — qualitative WORDS. Number of pets — quantitative NUMBERS. Both go in a FREQUENCY TABLE! Tally opens: 'WORDS go in QUAL, NUMBERS go in QUANT!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Detective Dot and Tally puppets. 'Friends — yesterday tree diagrams. Today FREQUENCY TABLES.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write FREQUENCY TABLE, QUALITATIVE, QUANTITATIVE on chart. 'Frequency = how often. Qualitative = words/categories. Quantitative = numbers.'

Demonstrate. Build a frequency table for QUALITATIVE data (favourite sport):

  Sport     | Frequency
  Hockey    | ||||CROSS ||||CROSS = 10
  Soccer    | ||||CROSS  = 5
  Baseball  | ||||  = 4
  Skiing    | || = 2

Now QUANTITATIVE (number of pets each child has):

  Pets | Frequency
  0    | ||||CROSS  = 5
  1    | ||||CROSS ||||CROSS = 10
  2    | ||| = 3
  3+   | || = 2

'Tally says — both kinds of data go in tables. Categories on left. Counts on right.'

More examples (Canadian flavour):
- 'Favourite season' qualitative.
- 'Number of snowy days last week' quantitative.
- 'Hockey team you cheer for' qualitative.
- 'Hours of TV per week' quantitative.

'Detective Dot says — qualitative = WORDS. Quantitative = NUMBERS. Both work the same in a frequency table.'

'Today YOU build 2 frequency tables: one of each kind.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: build a frequency table for 'favourite season' (8 students).
Three stations. A: Build qualitative table from survey. B: Build quantitative table from survey. C: Sort 6 questions as qualitative or quantitative.
Stretch at C: invent 3 of each kind.

INVENT-AND-COMPARE: Pairs design TWO different frequency table layouts for the same survey. Class compares: which makes totals easier? Cite Lehrer & Schauble (2002) — recording structure affects analysis.
steps.teacher_prompt: Tally: 'Same survey, different layouts. Pick the one your future self can read.'

differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at C: invent 3 of each.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Sentence frame: 'My data is QUAL or QUANT because ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children stand in line by their answers; teacher tallies. NO-PAPER PATH: children stand in two lines (QUAL line vs QUANT line) when teacher calls out a survey value. Body becomes the frequency table.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: builds frequency table; distinguishes qual/quant; counts correctly.

discussion_prompts: Why do we tally before counting?
consolidation.exit_routine: Tally's table refrain — 'Tally's rule: WORDS go in QUAL, NUMBERS go in QUANT!' (3x). Each child writes one row in each table from their survey.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child confuses QUALITATIVE and QUANTITATIVE — repairing the data-type mix-up at Grade 3
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On qualitative vs quantitative classification, the Grade-3 trap is treating numerical values as qualitative (e.g., 'age 7' as a label category rather than a quantity). Lehrer & Schauble (2002) and NCTM data trajectories place qual/quant distinction as the frequency-table prerequisite.

Yesterday Dot's branches were qualitative attributes. Today we distinguish QUAL (words/labels) from QUANT (numbers/measurements) and tabulate. Lesson 3 bar graphs; Lesson 4 mean/mode; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at C. Question 'favourite number'. Child says QUALITATIVE.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Tally asks — what KIND of value would each child give? A NUMBER like 7 or 23. That's QUANTITATIVE.'

Guide. 'Qualitative = words/categories (red, hockey, summer). Quantitative = numbers (7, 23, 100).'

Generlise. 'Tally says — look at the VALUES. Words = qual. Numbers = quant.'

If still confused: provide examples chart.
expected_student_responses: (Stretched) Catches edge cases (number-of-letters in name = quant).
common_misconceptions: Words = always qualitative regardless of subject. (Repair: look at value type.)
Numbers = always quantitative. (Repair: usually yes, but check.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child names a number but calls it qualitative: drill 'point to the VALUE — is it a NUMBER you could AVERAGE? Then it's QUANT.'
DIAGNOSTIC B — child sees a label and calls it quant: drill the opposite — 'words in QUAL, numbers in QUANT.'
DIAGNOSTIC C — child gets it but can't tabulate: side-by-side model — qual table + quant table for the same survey.

parts_outline.task: Sort 6 survey questions as QUAL or QUANT.
Build a frequency table from a tally chart.
Make your own qualitative + quantitative survey.
